lessons.title: Preventive Maintenance Schedules for African Work Conditions
lessons.body: Preventive maintenance is the backbone of profitable machinery operation in Africa. Dust, heat, humidity, and long supply chains punish equipment that is serviced only when it breaks. A planned schedule turns repair from an emergency into a routine cost. Start by building a machine register. For every unit record the make, model, serial number, year, engine or motor rating, fuel type, and current hour meter reading. Then create a maintenance calendar based on hours, not weeks. In dusty conditions service intervals shrink by twenty to thirty percent. A tractor working in Sahelian dust may need air filter cleaning every eight hours and replacement every one hundred hours, while the same machine in a coastal workshop could run longer. Lubrication is your cheapest insurance. Grease points on loaders, excavators, and trailers should be serviced daily before the first start. Use a manual grease gun if power is unreliable. Keep a laminated chart on the machine showing every nipple location. Engine oil and filter changes follow the manufacturer interval, but check oil daily with the dipstick. If oil looks black and gritty after fifty hours, change it early. Coolant matters in hot climates. A fifty fifty mix of antifreeze and clean water raises the boiling point and prevents corrosion. In areas with hard borehole water use distilled or filtered water. Check the radiator fins for dust and chaff. Blow them out with compressed air weekly. Fuel quality is a major cause of injector failure. Buy from reputable stations, allow fuel to settle in a drum for twenty four hours, and drain water from the bottom before filling. Install a water separator and change its element monthly. Hydraulic systems need clean fluid. Check levels daily and inspect hoses for cracks or weeping fittings. A burst hose can cost a day of production. Replace hoses at the first sign of abrasion. Track maintenance with a simple logbook or a phone app. Record date, hour meter, work done, parts used, and cost. Review the log monthly to spot repeat failures. If the same bearing fails three times, the root cause is misalignment or overload, not bad luck. Budget for maintenance. A common rule is to set aside three to five percent of the machine purchase price each year. For a used excavator bought at forty thousand dollars that is twelve hundred to two thousand dollars annually. Put this money in a separate account. When a hydraulic pump fails you will have cash to buy a replacement instead of losing a week waiting for a loan. Train operators to do daily checks. A ten minute walk around before start up catches low oil, loose bolts, and tyre damage. Give operators a checklist and a pen. Reward them for reporting faults early. In many African workshops the operator is also the mechanic. Cross training pays. Teach operators how to change filters, bleed fuel systems, and adjust tracks. Keep a critical spares list. For each machine identify the five parts that stop work when they fail. For a generator that might be fuel filter, air filter, oil filter, water pump belt, and battery. Stock these on site. For a truck it might be fan belt, brake pads, clutch fluid, wheel bearings, and fuel lift pump. Source locally where possible but keep one genuine spare of each critical item. Build relationships with two suppliers so you are not stranded when one runs out. Use condition monitoring. Touch bearings to feel for heat. Listen for unusual noises. Smell for burning rubber or hot oil. Look for leaks, cracks, and loose guards. These senses are free and effective. Vibration analysis and oil sampling are useful for large fleets but not essential for small operations. Finally, schedule major overhauls during low season. If you run a maize mill, service the engine before harvest when demand is low. If you run a bus, do the gearbox overhaul during school holidays. Preventive maintenance is not a cost centre. It is a profit centre. Every hour of planned service prevents ten hours of breakdown. In Africa where a breakdown can mean lost contracts, spoiled produce, and unpaid wages, the disciplined operator wins.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Diesel Engines in Remote Locations
lessons.body: Diesel engines power most African machinery because they are tough, fuel efficient, and torquey. But when they fail far from a dealer, you must diagnose with basic tools and clear thinking. Start with the three essentials: fuel, air, and compression. If an engine cranks but will not start, check fuel first. Open the bleed screw on the fuel filter housing and crank the engine. If no fuel pulses out, you have a supply problem. Check the tank for diesel and contamination. Look for a blocked fuel filter. In dusty conditions filters clog fast. Replace the primary and secondary filters. Then bleed the system from tank to injection pump. Loosen the bleed screw on the pump and crank until bubble free fuel appears. Tighten and try to start. If the engine starts then dies, you have an air leak on the suction side. Inspect all rubber fuel lines for cracks. Tighten hose clamps. A temporary fix is to wrap the line with self amalgamating tape. If fuel reaches the injectors but the engine still will not fire, check the stop solenoid. Many diesel engines have a solenoid that cuts fuel when the key is off. If it fails closed the engine gets no fuel. You can hear it click when the key is turned. If no click, test for voltage at the solenoid. If voltage is present but no click, replace the solenoid. In an emergency you can remove the plunger to get the engine running but you must stall the engine to stop it. Next check air. Remove the air filter element. If it is clogged with dust the engine will lack power and may not start. Clean it by tapping gently or blow with compressed air from the inside out. Never wash paper filters. If the filter is torn replace it. Check the intake hoses for cracks or loose clamps. A leaking intake after the filter lets in unfiltered air and causes rapid wear. Compression is the hardest to check in the field. If the engine cranks unevenly or blows white smoke, you may have a blown head gasket or worn rings. A quick test is to remove the oil filler cap while cranking. If you feel strong pulses of air, compression is escaping past the rings. If the engine overheats and loses coolant with no external leak, suspect a head gasket. In a remote site you can sometimes limp along by retorquing the head bolts and adding a sealant to the coolant. This is a temporary fix only. Order a gasket kit and plan a top overhaul. Overheating is a common killer. Check the radiator for blockage. Mud, chaff, and insects block fins. Clean with water and compressed air. Check the fan belt tension. A loose belt slips and the engine overheats. Tighten to about half an inch deflection. Check the thermostat. In an emergency you can remove it but the engine will run cold and wear faster. Check the water pump for play and leaks. If the bearing is gone replace the pump. Never open a hot radiator cap. Let the engine cool. Use a rag and release the cap slowly. If the engine runs rough and knocks, you may have injector problems. Diesel injectors need clean fuel and regular servicing. A stuck injector can wash cylinder walls and dilute oil. Remove injectors and have them tested at a workshop. In the field you can swap injectors between cylinders to see if the miss follows the injector. If it does, replace or repair that injector. Black smoke means too much fuel or not enough air. Check the air filter and turbo boost if fitted. Blue smoke means burning oil. Check the breather and valve guides. White smoke means unburnt fuel or coolant. Check injector timing and head gasket. Keep a basic tool kit. You need spanners from eight to twenty four millimetres, a set of screwdrivers, pliers, a hammer, a hacksaw, a file, a multimeter, a compression tester, and a timing light if applicable. Also carry spare filters, fuel lines, hose clamps, gasket paper, and a tube of silicone. In Africa you often cannot buy a single bolt at midnight. Your spares box is your lifeline. Document every fault and fix. Write in a notebook the symptoms, what you checked, what you changed, and the result. Over time you build a diagnostic map for your machines. Share this knowledge with your team. A mechanic who understands the fuel system can save a day of downtime. Finally, know when to stop. If you lack the parts or skill, call a specialist. A botched repair can destroy an engine. The goal is to get running safely and cheaply, not to prove you can fix everything alone.

lessons.title: Hydraulic System Repair and Contamination Control
lessons.body: Hydraulics give African machinery its muscle. Excavators, loaders, backhoes, and presses rely on pressurised oil to move heavy loads. When hydraulics fail the machine is dead. Most failures are caused by contamination, heat, or incorrect pressure. Learn to control these three and you will save thousands. Start with cleanliness. Dirt is the enemy. A grain of sand smaller than a pinhead can score a pump or jam a valve. Always clean around any fitting before you open it. Use a pressure washer or a brush and rags. Plug open ports with clean caps or tape. Never use a rag that sheds lint. Use lint free cloths. When you change hydraulic oil, filter it before use. Store oil in clean sealed drums. Use a hand pump with a filter. If you must use a funnel, clean it first. Change hydraulic filters at the recommended interval. In dusty conditions change them more often. A clogged filter causes the pump to cavitate, which sounds like marbles rattling. Cavitation destroys pumps quickly. If you hear that noise, stop the machine and change the filter. Check the suction strainer in the tank. Clean it with diesel and a soft brush. Never use a wire brush that leaves metal particles. Water is another contaminant. Condensation forms in hydraulic tanks when they heat and cool. In humid African climates this happens daily. Drain water from the bottom of the tank weekly. Install a breather with a desiccant if available. If oil looks milky, it has water. You must drain and flush the system. Heat shortens oil life. Hydraulic oil should run between sixty and eighty degrees Celsius. If it is too hot, check the cooler. Clean the cooler fins. Check the fan. Ensure the relief valve is not stuck open. A stuck relief valve sends oil back to tank at high pressure and generates heat. Test relief pressure with a gauge. If it is low, adjust or replace the valve. If it is high, the pump works too hard and heat rises. Follow the manufacturer specification. Hoses and fittings fail often. Inspect hoses for cracks, blisters, and abrasion. Replace any hose that shows the reinforcement wires. A burst hose under pressure can inject oil into your skin, which is a medical emergency. Never check for leaks with your hand. Use a piece of cardboard or wood. If a fitting leaks, tighten it. If it still leaks, replace the O ring or the fitting. Use the correct size and material. Hydraulic seals come in nitrile, viton, and polyurethane. Use the right one for the oil and temperature. Cylinders need attention. If a cylinder drifts under load, the piston seal is worn. If it leaks externally, the rod seal is worn. Rebuild kits are available for most cylinders. To rebuild, remove the cylinder, drain the oil, and unscrew the end cap. Use a spanner or a chain wrench. Pull out the piston and rod. Inspect the bore for scores. If scored deeply, replace the cylinder or have it honed. Replace all seals and the wear ring. Lubricate with clean hydraulic oil before reassembly. Torque the end cap to specification. Bleed the cylinder by cycling it slowly several times. Valves and pumps are precision parts. Do not open them unless you have a clean bench and the right tools. A pump that is worn will have low flow and the machine will be slow. Test flow with a flow meter. If flow is below specification, replace or rebuild the pump. Control valves can stick due to contamination. Sometimes you can free them by cycling the control many times. If not, remove the valve spool and clean it with solvent and compressed air. Replace any damaged O rings. Always depressurise the system before working on it. Turn off the engine and cycle the controls to release trapped pressure. Lock out the machine so no one starts it. Use a pressure gauge to confirm zero pressure. Keep a hydraulic schematic for each machine. It shows component locations and flow paths. Without it you are guessing. Train your team on contamination control. Provide clean work areas, clean rags, and caps. Make it a rule that no one opens a hydraulic line without cleaning first. The cost of a pump is ten times the cost of a filter. In Africa where parts take weeks to arrive, prevention is not optional. It is survival.

lessons.title: Electrical Fault Finding on Mobile and Stationary Machinery
lessons.body: Electrical problems stop machines as surely as mechanical ones. In Africa, voltage fluctuations, dust, moisture, and poor wiring cause many faults. Learn a logical approach and you can fix most issues with a multimeter and basic tools. Start with the battery. A weak battery cranks slowly or not at all. Check the terminals for corrosion. Clean with a wire brush and apply petroleum jelly. Check the electrolyte level in lead acid batteries. Top up with distilled water only. Check the voltage with a multimeter. A fully charged twelve volt battery reads about twelve point six volts engine off. While cranking it should not drop below ten volts. If it does, charge or replace the battery. Check the alternator. With the engine running, battery voltage should be thirteen point eight to fourteen point four volts. If it is lower, the alternator is not charging. Check the belt tension. Check the wiring to the alternator. If the warning light stays on, the alternator may have a failed diode or regulator. Remove and test or replace. Next check fuses and relays. A blown fuse is easy to miss. Use a test light or multimeter to check both sides of the fuse. If power is on one side but not the other, replace the fuse. Never use a higher rated fuse. That can cause a fire. Relays click when they work. If a relay does not click, swap it with a known good one. Check the socket for corrosion. Wiring is a common failure point. Vibration, heat, and rodents damage insulation. Look for chafed wires, especially where they pass through metal panels. Use a wiring diagram. If you do not have one, trace the circuit from the battery to the component. Check for voltage at each connector. A voltage drop test is better than a simple voltage check. Set the multimeter to DC volts and measure across a connection while the circuit is under load. More than zero point five volts drop means a bad connection. Clean and tighten. Grounds are critical. A bad ground causes strange faults. Clean the frame ground and the engine ground. Use star washers and dielectric grease. Sensors and solenoids fail. A solenoid that does not click may have no power or a bad coil. Test for power at the connector. If power is present, test the coil resistance. If it is open or shorted, replace. Sensors like coolant temperature, oil pressure, and position sensors can cause the engine to derate or shut down. If you have a diagnostic tool, read the fault codes. If not, test the sensor resistance against a known value. Many sensors are variable resistors. As temperature or pressure changes, resistance changes. If it does not, replace. Starters can fail. If you hear a click but no crank, the starter solenoid may be bad or the battery is weak. If you hear nothing, check the ignition switch and the neutral safety switch. On many machines the starter will not engage unless the transmission is in neutral or the clutch is pressed. Bypass the switch temporarily to test. If the starter spins but does not engage the flywheel, the drive is bad. Remove and repair or replace. Lighting and accessories are simpler. Check bulbs, then fuses, then switches, then wiring. Use a test light to follow the circuit. For trailers and implements, check the connector pins for corrosion. Clean and apply dielectric grease. In dusty conditions, use sealed connectors and heat shrink tubing. Keep moisture out. Use cable ties to secure wires away from hot and moving parts. Add a drip loop where wires enter a box so water runs off. Label wires at both ends. This saves hours later. Keep a wiring diagram in the cab. If you do not have one, draw your own as you trace. Use a multimeter daily. Learn to measure volts, ohms, and continuity. Practice on a known good circuit. In Africa, power quality is often poor. Use a surge protector for stationary machinery. For generators, check the voltage and frequency. If the voltage is too high, the AVR may be faulty. If frequency is low, the engine speed is low. Adjust the governor. Finally, safety. Always disconnect the battery before working on electrical systems. Use insulated tools. Never work on live circuits in wet conditions. If you are unsure, call an auto electrician. A small fault can become a fire. The goal is to restore function safely and cheaply, not to become an electrician overnight.

lessons.title: Starting and Running a Machinery Repair Business in Africa
lessons.body: Turning repair skills into a business requires more than technical ability. You need customers, cash flow, and a reputation for reliability. Start by defining your niche. Do you repair tractors, generators, trucks, or construction equipment? Specialising lets you stock the right parts and train your team. In a region with many maize farmers, tractor and trailer repair is steady work. Near a mine, focus on loaders and excavators. Near a city, focus on generators and small plant. Next, set up a simple workshop. You do not need a concrete palace. You need a level area, a roof for shade, a strong bench, a vice, and secure storage for tools and parts. Invest in a good tool kit. Buy quality spanners, sockets, torque wrenches, and a multimeter. Cheap tools break and injure. Add a compressor, a grease gun, a hydraulic jack, and axle stands. For field work, keep a mobile kit in a sturdy box. Include common filters, belts, hoses, clamps, wire, and fuses. Keep a notebook for every job. Record customer name, machine, fault, work done, parts used, labour hours, and payment. This helps you price future jobs and track debtors. Pricing is critical. Many African mechanics undercharge and then cannot buy parts. Calculate your costs. Add labour, parts markup, transport, and a profit margin. Labour rates vary. In a rural area you might charge ten to twenty dollars per hour. In a city, thirty to fifty. For a field call out, charge for travel. For emergency work at night or on weekends, charge a premium. Always give a written quote before starting. If the job is complex, quote a diagnostic fee. This filters serious customers. Get a deposit for parts. Never use your own money to buy parts for a customer unless you trust them. Build a network of parts suppliers. Visit them. Negotiate discounts for bulk or regular purchases. Keep a list of alternative suppliers for common parts. When a customer needs a part urgently, you can call around. If you cannot find it, consider rebuilding or fabricating. Many African workshops survive by machining bushes, welding brackets, and making gaskets. Learn these skills or hire someone who has them. Marketing is word of mouth. Do good work and ask satisfied customers to refer you. Leave a sticker with your phone number on the machine. Join local farmer or transport associations. Attend trade shows. Use WhatsApp to share photos of your work. Create a simple business card. Keep your phone charged and answer calls. Reliability is your brand. If you say you will come at eight, be there at eight. If you cannot, call. Customers forgive delays but not silence. Manage cash flow. Repair businesses fail because they buy parts on credit and customers pay late. Invoice immediately. Follow up politely. Offer a small discount for early payment. Keep a reserve for slow months. Train apprentices. In Africa, skilled mechanics are scarce. Take on one or two young people. Teach them safety, tool care, and diagnostic thinking. Pay them a stipend. They will become your best workers. Use technology. A smartphone can take photos of faults, send quotes, and track payments. Use a simple accounting app or a notebook. Record every expense. At the end of the month, calculate profit. If you are not making money, raise prices or cut costs. Safety is non negotiable. Use gloves, goggles, and steel toe boots. Jack up safely. Disconnect batteries. Never work under a machine held only by a jack. Keep a first aid kit. Fire extinguishers are cheap compared to a burned workshop. Insurance is difficult in many African markets but try to insure your tools and workshop. Finally, think long term. Reinvest profits in tools, training, and a bigger workshop. Build a team. Move from doing every job yourself to managing others. The goal is a business that runs without you. That is true success. A machinery repair business can support a family, employ others, and keep Africa moving. Start small, be honest, and never stop learning.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a lockout tagout procedure before repairing machinery?
options: B) To isolate hazardous energy sources
quiz.explanation: Lockout tagout isolates hazardous energy to prevent accidental startup or release of energy during repair.

quiz.q: Which document should be consulted first to identify the correct repair procedure for a specific machine?
quiz.explanation: The manufacturer service manual provides the approved procedures, specifications, and torque values for that machine.

quiz.q: What does a bearing temperature rise above normal most likely indicate?
options: D) Friction from wear or misalignment
quiz.explanation: Elevated bearing temperature usually signals friction caused by wear, poor lubrication, or misalignment.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for measuring the clearance between a valve tappet and a rocker arm?
quiz.explanation: A feeler gauge is a set of thin metal strips used to measure small gaps such as valve clearances.

quiz.q: What is the correct action if a machine vibrates excessively after reassembly?
options: A) Increase operating speed to smooth it out
B) Shut down and inspect for imbalance or loose parts
C) Ignore it until the next scheduled service
D) Add more grease to all fittings
quiz.explanation: Excessive vibration after reassembly requires immediate shutdown and inspection to prevent damage or injury.

quiz.q: Which type of maintenance is performed based on elapsed operating hours or calendar time?
quiz.explanation: Preventive maintenance follows a fixed schedule based on time or usage to avoid unexpected failures.

quiz.q: What should be done with used hydraulic oil during a repair?
options: A) Pour it down a drain
B) Mix it with regular trash
C) Store it in a labeled container for proper disposal
D) Reuse it indefinitely without testing
quiz.explanation: Used hydraulic oil is hazardous waste and must be stored in labeled containers and disposed of according to regulations.

quiz.q: Which safety practice is required before removing a guard from a machine?
options: A) Speed up the machine to finish faster
B) Ask a coworker to hold the guard
C) Remove the guard while the machine runs
D) De-energize and lock out the machine
quiz.explanation: Guards must only be removed after the machine is de-energized and locked out to prevent injury.
